claim: Haematopoiesis occurs in the limb bones of most tetrapods.
source: The production of blood cells (haematopoiesis) occurs in the limb bones of most tetrapods but is absent in the fin bones of ray-finned fish.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general biological fact about tetrapods.

claim: Haematopoiesis is absent in the fin bones of ray-finned fish.
source: The production of blood cells (haematopoiesis) occurs in the limb bones of most tetrapods but is absent in the fin bones of ray-finned fish.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general biological fact about ray-finned fish.

claim: Recent hypotheses suggested that haematopoiesis migrated into long bones prior to the water-to-land transition.
source: Recent hypotheses suggested that haematopoiesis migrated into long bones prior to the water-to-land transition and protected newly-produced blood cells from harsher environmental conditions.
evidence: This claim references existing hypotheses in the literature, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Little fossil evidence to support hypotheses about haematopoiesis migration has been provided so far.
source: However, little fossil evidence to support these hypotheses has been provided so far.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field presented in the abstract.

claim: Permian tetrapods seem to be among the first to exhibit a centralised marrow organisation.
source: They show that Permian tetrapods seem to be among the first to exhibit a centralised marrow organisation, which allows haematopoiesis as in extant amniotes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's observations.

claim: Centralised marrow organisation allows haematopoiesis as in extant amniotes.
source: They show that Permian tetrapods seem to be among the first to exhibit a centralised marrow organisation, which allows haematopoiesis as in extant amniotes.
evidence: This connects the observed marrow organisation to its functional capability based on comparison with extant amniotes.

claim: Long-bone haematopoiesis was probably not an exaptation to the water-to-land transition.
source: Not only does our study demonstrate that long-bone haematopoiesis was probably not an exaptation to the water-to-land transition but it sheds light on the early evolution of limb-bone development and the sequence of bone-marrow functional acquisitions.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Tetrapod long bones are among the most studied skeletal elements in the field of bone biology.
source: Tetrapod long bones are among the most studied skeletal elements in the field of bone biology as they constitute a unit of reference for understanding the development and biomechanics of the appendicular skeleton (e.g. Duboule, 1994; Fröbisch, 2008; Hall, 2008; Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Fossil tetrapod trackways suggested that limbs supported weight and engaged substrate locomotion earlier than previously thought in early tetrapod evolution.
source: The recent discovery of fossil tetrapod trackways (Ahlberg, 2018; Niedźwiedzki et al., 2010) suggested that limbs supported weight and engaged substrate locomotion earlier than previously thought in early tetrapod evolution.
evidence: This is supported by citations to trackway discoveries.

claim: Long bones host bone marrow including stem-cell niches for the production of blood cells.
source: Not only crucial for their biomechanical properties, long bones also host bone marrow including stem-cell niches for the production of blood cells, that is haematopoiesis (Orkin and Zon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orkin and Zon, 2008.

claim: After birth, bone marrow is the definitive haematopoietic system in mostly terrestrial mammals and many other tetrapods.
source: After birth, bone marrow is the definitive haematopoietic system in mostly terrestrial mammals and many other tetrapods (Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012; Kapp et al., 2018; Orkin and Zon, 2008) but not in fish or some aquatic tetrapods (Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012; Avagyan and Zon, 2016; Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Bone marrow is not the definitive haematopoietic system in fish or some aquatic tetrapods.
source: After birth, bone marrow is the definitive haematopoietic system in mostly terrestrial mammals and many other tetrapods (Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012; Kapp et al., 2018; Orkin and Zon, 2008) but not in fish or some aquatic tetrapods (Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012; Avagyan and Zon, 2016; Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Red blood cells are produced in the supraspinal organ in the lamprey.
source: Indeed, red blood cells are produced in the supraspinal organ in the lamprey, the kidney and liver in actinopterygians (ray-finned fish) and some amphibians (tadpoles and aquatic adults, Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012), and the kidney in lungfish (Amemiya et al., 2007; Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Red blood cells are produced in the kidney and liver in actinopterygians and some amphibians.
source: Indeed, red blood cells are produced in the supraspinal organ in the lamprey, the kidney and liver in actinopterygians (ray-finned fish) and some amphibians (tadpoles and aquatic adults, Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012), and the kidney in lungfish (Amemiya et al., 2007; Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Red blood cells are produced in the kidney in lungfish.
source: Indeed, red blood cells are produced in the supraspinal organ in the lamprey, the kidney and liver in actinopterygians (ray-finned fish) and some amphibians (tadpoles and aquatic adults, Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012), and the kidney in lungfish (Amemiya et al., 2007; Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The skeleton would have played a major role in protecting blood-cell production against temperature changes over the water-to-land transition.
source: Several studies proposed that the skeleton would have played a major role in hosting blood-cell production over the water-to-land transition and (1) protecting it against temperature changes (Weiss and Wislocki, 1956), (2) protecting it against potential DNA mutations induced by UV exposure on land (Horton, 1980; Kapp et al., 2018) or (3) providing a better efficiency in red-blood-cell production necessary for metabolically-demanding terrestrial locomotion and aerial respiration (Tanaka, 1976).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The skeleton would have played a major role in protecting blood-cell production against potential DNA mutations induced by UV exposure on land.
source: Several studies proposed that the skeleton would have played a major role in hosting blood-cell production over the water-to-land transition and (1) protecting it against temperature changes (Weiss and Wislocki, 1956), (2) protecting it against potential DNA mutations induced by UV exposure on land (Horton, 1980; Kapp et al., 2018) or (3) providing a better efficiency in red-blood-cell production necessary for metabolically-demanding terrestrial locomotion and aerial respiration (Tanaka, 1976).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The skeleton would have provided better efficiency in red-blood-cell production necessary for metabolically-demanding terrestrial locomotion and aerial respiration.
source: Several studies proposed that the skeleton would have played a major role in hosting blood-cell production over the water-to-land transition and (1) protecting it against temperature changes (Weiss and Wislocki, 1956), (2) protecting it against potential DNA mutations induced by UV exposure on land (Horton, 1980; Kapp et al., 2018) or (3) providing a better efficiency in red-blood-cell production necessary for metabolically-demanding terrestrial locomotion and aerial respiration (Tanaka, 1976).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: Tetrapod long bones are regionalised in three parts mirrored from midshaft: diaphysis, metaphyses, and epiphyses.
source: Tetrapod long bones are regionalised in three parts mirrored from midshaft (Figure 1): (1) the middle of the shaft is called diaphysis; (2) the metaphyses are located at each extremity of the shaft and (3) the epiphyses start above the ossification notch (i.e. where the cortical bone stops forming), extend beyond the metaphyses, and comprise one or more condyles in the case of concave articulations (Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Long bones elongate from the growth plate, which is located in the metaphysis.
source: Long bones elongate from the growth plate, which is located in the metaphysis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 and represents established knowledge.

claim: In the metaphysis, cartilage is progressively substituted with bone through endochondral ossification.
source: In this region, the cartilage is progressively substituted with bone: this process is called endochondral ossification (Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990; Hall, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: In extant amniotes, long-bone elongation results from the proliferation of longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cartilage cells.
source: In extant amniotes, long-bone elongation results from the proliferation of longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cartilage cells, called hypertrophic chondrocytes (Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990; Haines, 1942; Xie et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Hypertrophic chondrocytes express collagen type X which facilitates the calcification of the surrounding matrix.
source: The latter express collagen type X which facilitates the calcification of the surrounding matrix (Gudmann and Karsdal, 2016; Lüllmann-Rauch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Hypertrophic chondrocytes secrete matrix vesicles containing calcium phosphate crystals.
source: To do so, the hypertrophic chondrocytes secrete matrix vesicles containing calcium phosphate crystals (Amizuka, 2012; Anderson and Shapiro, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The vesicles align longitudinally along the septa.
source: The vesicles align longitudinally along the septa.
evidence: This is stated as part of the description of the process.

claim: The crystals penetrate the vesicle membranes to form stellate clusters of needle-shaped apatite in the extra cellular matrix.
source: The crystals penetrate the vesicle membranes to form stellate clusters of needle-shaped apatite in the extra cellular matrix (Amizuka, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The mineralisation propagates following the longitudinal organisation of the septa.
source: The mineralisation thus propagates following the longitudinal organisation of the septa (Amizuka, 2012; Anderson and Shapiro, 2010; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Blood vessels and marrow processes invade the growth plate along columns of hypertrophic cartilage.
source: Blood vessels and marrow processes invade the growth plate along these columns of hypertrophic cartilage (Lüllmann-Rauch, 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Lytic enzymes secreted by bone-marrow cells degrade the cartilage matrix, which is progressively substituted by bone deposition.
source: Lytic enzymes secreted by the bone-marrow cells degrade the cartilage matrix, which is progressively substituted by bone deposition (Lüllmann-Rauch, 2015; Suzuki et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: VEGF triggers cartilage calcification and regulates endochondral ossification through stimulation of blood-vessel ingrowth into the diaphysis.
source: Growth factors, such as the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), trigger cartilage calcification and regulate endochondral ossification through stimulation of blood-vessel ingrowth into the diaphysis (Gerber et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Lines of calcifying stellate clusters of crystals form a scaffold for future trabecular bone deposition.
source: The lines of calcifying stellate clusters of crystals therefore form a scaffold for future trabecular bone deposition (Amizuka, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The calcifying stellate clusters result in the formation of a bony mesh of longitudinal trabeculae.
source: This results in the formation of a bony mesh of longitudinal trabeculae (Figure 1A), which is progressively incorporated into the metaphysis where haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niches (Figure 1A) are located (Calvi et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2003) in the close vicinity of trabecular/endothelial surfaces (Gong, 1978; Nilsson et al., 2001; Wilson and Trumpp, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: HSC niches are located in the metaphysis in the close vicinity of trabecular/endothelial surfaces.
source: This results in the formation of a bony mesh of longitudinal trabeculae (Figure 1A), which is progressively incorporated into the metaphysis where haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niches (Figure 1A) are located (Calvi et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2003) in the close vicinity of trabecular/endothelial surfaces (Gong, 1978; Nilsson et al., 2001; Wilson and Trumpp, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: HSC form localised niches whose environment is greatly controlled and regulated.
source: HSC form localised niches whose environment is greatly controlled and regulated (Orkin and Zon, 2008; Sipkins et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Haematopoiesis only occurs in long bones whose shafts are greatly opened.
source: For that reason, haematopoiesis only occurs in long bones whose shafts are greatly opened (Bazzini et al., 1986; Tanaka, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In most amniotes, the trabecular mesh in the metaphysis can be vastly remodelled.
source: In most amniotes, the trabecular mesh in the metaphysis can be vastly remodelled (Haines, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Often in mature animals the growth plate disappears, causing the senescence of long-bone elongation.
source: Often in mature animals the growth plate disappears, causing the senescence of long-bone elongation (Kilborn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: HSC can be observed adjacent to epiphyseal trabeculae after growth plate remodelling.
source: HSC can thereafter be observed adjacent to epiphyseal trabeculae (Askenasy and Farkas, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The elongation of limb bones in extant urodeles differs from the process in amniotes.
source: In extant urodeles (e.g. Pleurodeles waltl, De Ricqlès, 1964; De Ricqlès, 1965), the elongation of limb bones differs from the process in amniotes (Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990; Haines, 1938; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Endochondral ossification starts at a later stage in urodeles than in mammals.
source: Unlike mammals, endochondral ossification starts at a later stage in urodeles (De Ricqlès, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The diaphyseal cartilaginous matrix is first hollowed by the formation of lacunae that are subsequently filled in with bone marrow in urodeles.
source: The diaphyseal cartilaginous matrix is first hollowed by the formation of lacunae that are subsequently filled in with bone marrow, far before endochondral ossification starts (De Ricqlès, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In mammals and birds, VEGF initiates vascular ingrowth before endochondral ossification starts.
source: In mammals and birds (e.g. mouse, Zelzer et al., 2002; chicken, Carlevaro et al., 2000), VEGF initiates vascular ingrowth before endochondral ossification starts.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A peak of VEGF expression is present in the hindlimb of Bufo gargarizan at metamorphic climax.
source: In the amphibian Bufo gargarizan, a peak of VEGF expression is present in the hindlimb at metamorphic climax (Gao et al., 2018) paralleling an increase of endochondral ossification activity (Bo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: VEGF would seem to play a major role in amphibian long-bone endochondral ossification.
source: VEGF would therefore seem to play a major role in amphibian long-bone endochondral ossification as well, but this role still needs to be characterised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the VEGF expression data.

claim: The growth plate in the metaphysis of urodeles exhibits no aligned columns of hypertrophic cartilage cells or drastically reduced alignment of a few cells at most.
source: The growth plate in the metaphysis of urodeles exhibits no aligned columns of hypertrophic cartilage cells or drastically reduced alignment of a few cells at most (De Ricqlès, 1965; Dickson, 1982; Felisbino and Carvalho, 1999; Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: In urodeles, aligned columns of hypertrophic cartilage do not constitute the location where ossification takes place.
source: Contrary to amniotes, when present, these aligned columns of hypertrophic cartilage do not constitute the location where the ossification takes place (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to amniotes and referenced to Figure 1B.

claim: In urodeles, the mineralisation front is located in the underlying areas of the growth plate.
source: Instead, the mineralisation front is located in the underlying areas of the growth plate (i.e. in a layer of non-oriented hypertrophic cartilage or stratified non-oriented hypertrophic cartilage, De Ricqlès, 1965).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In urodeles, mineralisation occurs via the formation of globular structures called globuli ossei.
source: There, after erosion of the cartilage, mineralisation occurs in urodeles via the formation of globular structures called globuli ossei (Figure 1B; De Ricqlès, 1965; Quilhac et al., 2014) and spherical mineralisation around them (forming Liesegang's rings, Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Globuli ossei are either opened hypertrophic cartilaginous cells which died and were subsequently invaded by a cell from the blood/marrow system to initiate mineralisation or uneroded hypertrophic cartilaginous cells modified into active cells which synthesise bone-like collagen fibrils.
source: Globuli ossei are either (1) opened hypertrophic cartilaginous cells which died and were subsequently invaded by a cell from the blood/marrow system to initiate mineralisation or (2) uneroded hypertrophic cartilaginous cells modified into active cells which synthesise bone-like collagen fibrils (of intermediate size between type II of the cartilage and type I of the bone, Quilhac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Endochondral ossification in urodeles does not produce a longitudinally-oriented trabecular network.
source: The endochondral ossification therefore does not produce a longitudinally-oriented trabecular network (Figure 1B), but forms instead a light reticular mesh (De Ricqlès, 1965; Quilhac et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2008), rich in globuli ossei (De Ricqlès, 1964; Haines, 1938; Quilhac et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The epiphyses of urodeles remain cartilaginous while they often ossify in anurans.
source: The epiphyses of urodeles remain cartilaginous while they often ossify in anurans (Castanet et al., 2003; Francillon, 1981; Sanchez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Epiphyseal ossification in anurans is probably an adaptation to demanding jumping locomotion and/or heterochronic mechanisms relevant to this clade.
source: This is probably an adaptation to a demanding jumping locomotion and/or heterochronic mechanisms relevant to this clade (Francillon, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents an interpretation.

claim: In the medullary cavity of anuran long bones, cartilaginous cells hypertrophy with no preferential orientation as in urodeles.
source: In the medullary cavity of their long bones however, the cartilaginous cells hypertrophy with no preferential orientation as in urodeles (Dickson, 1982; Felisbino and Carvalho, 1999; Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001; Miura et al., 2008; Rozenblut and Ogielska, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The resulting spongiosa in anurans is largely reduced or quite often absent.
source: The resulting spongiosa is largely reduced (even quite often absent, Francillon, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The epiphyseal cartilage in anurans hangs over the ossification notch and the shaft.
source: The epiphyseal cartilage hangs over the ossification notch and the shaft (Francillon, 1981) to ossify straight after the metamorphosis (Miura et al., 2008; Rozenblut and Ogielska, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The function of bone marrow in amphibian long bones differs from the function in extant amniotes.
source: The function of bone marrow in amphibian long bones also differs from the function in extant amniotes.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation.

claim: In amphibians, the sites for haematopoiesis almost exclusively comprise the thymus, spleen and liver.
source: Indeed, in amphibians, the sites for haematopoiesis almost exclusively comprise the thymus, spleen and liver (Akiyoshi and Inoue, 2012; Hightower and Pierre, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Bone marrow only plays a role of haematopoiesis in a few amphibian species.
source: Bone marrow only plays a role of haematopoiesis in a few amphibian species (e.g. Xenopus laevis, Rana catesbeiana, Tanaka, 1976; Phillobates terribilis, Dendrobates tinctorius, Kapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In amphibians with bone marrow haematopoiesis, it occurs in endosteal regions of the diaphysis between sinusoids and endosteum.
source: In these cases, haematopoiesis occurs in endosteal regions of the diaphysis between sinusoids (i.e. fenestrated capillaries; Figure 1B2) and endosteum (Tanaka, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1B2.

claim: No HSC has been observed so far in the epiphysis of frogs.
source: No HSC has been observed so far in the epiphysis of frogs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: Some authors suggest that the amniote-like elongation process may have been the primitive state.
source: On the one hand, some authors suggest that the amniote-like elongation process may have been the primitive state (Haines, 1942) but no fossil evidence was provided.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Early tetrapods had cartilaginous epiphyses like extant urodeles.
source: On the other hand, early tetrapods had cartilaginous epiphyses like extant urodeles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: Palaeohistological studies revealed a fan-like longitudinal trabecular arrangement in the long-bone metaphysis of Eusthenopteron.
source: Recently, palaeohistological studies revealed a fan-like longitudinal trabecular arrangement in the long-bone metaphysis of the 380-million-year-old lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron (Sanchez et al., 2014), and in the 365-million-year-old limbed stem-tetrapod Acanthostega (Sanchez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Palaeohistological studies revealed a fan-like longitudinal trabecular arrangement in the long-bone metaphysis of Acanthostega.
source: Recently, palaeohistological studies revealed a fan-like longitudinal trabecular arrangement in the long-bone metaphysis of the 380-million-year-old lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron (Sanchez et al., 2014), and in the 365-million-year-old limbed stem-tetrapod Acanthostega (Sanchez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The fan-like trabecular patterns in Eusthenopteron and Acanthostega would result from the same elongation process as in amniotes.
source: These patterns would result from the same elongation process as in amniotes and would rather suggest that amphibians exhibit a derived condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns.

claim: The diaphyseal and metaphyseal microarchitectures of Eusthenopteron were described by Sanchez et al., 2014.
source: The diaphyseal and metaphyseal microarchitectures of the stem tetrapods Eusthenopteron and Hyneria were described by Sanchez et al., 2014 and Kamska et al., 2018, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The diaphyseal and metaphyseal microarchitectures of Hyneria were described by Kamska et al., 2018.
source: The diaphyseal and metaphyseal microarchitectures of the stem tetrapods Eusthenopteron and Hyneria were described by Sanchez et al., 2014 and Kamska et al., 2018, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus was thoroughly described by Sanchez et al., 2008.
source: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus (Sanchez et al., 2008), Apateon (Sanchez et al., 2010a; Sanchez et al., 2010b), Metoposaurus (Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013) and Seymouria (Estefa et al., 2020) were thoroughly described, but the metaphyseal organisation of their humeri was only succinctly mentioned in the cited articles.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The diaphysis of Apateon was thoroughly described by Sanchez et al., 2010a and 2010b.
source: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus (Sanchez et al., 2008), Apateon (Sanchez et al., 2010a; Sanchez et al., 2010b), Metoposaurus (Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013) and Seymouria (Estefa et al., 2020) were thoroughly described, but the metaphyseal organisation of their humeri was only succinctly mentioned in the cited articles.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The diaphysis of Metoposaurus was thoroughly described by Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013.
source: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus (Sanchez et al., 2008), Apateon (Sanchez et al., 2010a; Sanchez et al., 2010b), Metoposaurus (Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013) and Seymouria (Estefa et al., 2020) were thoroughly described, but the metaphyseal organisation of their humeri was only succinctly mentioned in the cited articles.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The diaphysis of Seymouria was thoroughly described by Estefa et al., 2020.
source: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus (Sanchez et al., 2008), Apateon (Sanchez et al., 2010a; Sanchez et al., 2010b), Metoposaurus (Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013) and Seymouria (Estefa et al., 2020) were thoroughly described, but the metaphyseal organisation of their humeri was only succinctly mentioned in the cited articles.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The metaphyseal organisation of Discosauriscus, Apateon, Metoposaurus and Seymouria humeri was only succinctly mentioned in previous articles.
source: The diaphysis of Discosauriscus (Sanchez et al., 2008), Apateon (Sanchez et al., 2010a; Sanchez et al., 2010b), Metoposaurus (Konietzko-Meier and Sander, 2013) and Seymouria (Estefa et al., 2020) were thoroughly described, but the metaphyseal organisation of their humeri was only succinctly mentioned in the cited articles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the literature.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 humerus, a relatively complete sequence of calcification extending over 600 µm can be described.
source: Nevertheless, a relatively complete sequence of calcification (extending over 600 µm) can be described here.
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 humerus, obvious figures of globuli ossei are entrapped in Liesegang's rings.
source: Under this region, obvious figures of globuli ossei are entrapped in Liesegang's rings (g.o. and l.r., Figure 2Bb1-2).
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 humerus, globuli ossei are numerous and unevenly arranged.
source: They are numerous and unevenly arranged.
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 humerus, globuli ossei sizes range from 9 to 15 µm in diameter.
source: Their sizes (ranging from 9 to 15 µm in diameter) seem as well unevenly distributed.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the specimen.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 humerus, trabeculae are very few.
source: The trabeculae are very few in this thin section (t., Figure 2Bb2).
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, large sequences of cartilage calcification spread over more than a third of the total bone length on each side.
source: Both bones exhibit large sequences of cartilage calcification which spread over more than a third of the total bone length on each side of the long bone (Figure 2C).

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, the mineralisation front is located relatively far under the ossification notch (400 µm).
source: The mineralisation front (m.f., Figure 2C) is located relatively far under the ossification notch (400 µm) (o.n., Figure 2C).

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, numerous globuli ossei can be visualised in the metaphysis.
source: Numerous globuli ossei can be visualised in the metaphysis (g.o., Figure 2Cc1,3).

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, globuli ossei are unevenly distributed and their size ranges between 8 and 25 µm.
source: They are unevenly distributed and their size ranges between 8 and 25 µm.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the specimen.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, clusters of chondrocytes can be observed.
source: Clusters of chondrocytes can be observed (c.c., Figure 2Cc3).
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, the top of the epiphysis probably exhibited a uniform matrix of uncalcified cartilage before fossilisation that was not preserved afterwards.
source: The top of the epiphysis probably exhibited a uniform matrix of uncalcified cartilage before the fossilisation that was not preserved afterwards.
evidence: This is an inference about the preservation state.

claim: In Apateon caducus juvenile specimen GPIM-N 1297 radius and ulna, the mesh of ossified trabeculae is very scattered and shows no preferential orientation.
source: The mesh of ossified trabeculae is very scattered and shows no preferential orientation (t., Figure 2Cc1).
evidence: This is based on observations of the specimen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Apateon caducus adult specimen GPIM-N 1572 radius and ulna, the epiphysis and metaphysis are more hollowed than those of specimen GPIM-N 1297.
source: The epiphysis and metaphysis of the radius and ulna of this individual (Figure 3A) are more hollowed than those of the specimen GPIM-N 1297, with less cartilaginous matrix between the mineralised trabeculae (Figure 3B).

source: Although all limb bones studied here have cartilaginous epiphyses, their metaphyseal organisation, and the underlying long-bone elongation processes, can greatly differ between taxa.
evidence: This is based on observations across all specimens.

claim: The long-bone elongation in Apateon probably results from the hypertrophying action of scattered cartilaginous cells in the upper part of the metaphysis.
source: The long-bone elongation in Apateon probably results from the hypertrophying action of scattered cartilaginous cells in the upper part of the metaphysis (Figure 11).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of Apateon specimens.

claim: The fossils of Apateon revealed a mineralisation front characterised by a large number of globuli ossei.
source: The fossils revealed a mineralisation front characterised by a large number of globuli ossei (Figures 2–5), which progressively replaced these hypertrophic chondrocytes, as in urodeles (De Ricqlès, 1964; De Ricqlès, 1965; Haines, 1938; Quilhac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on observations of Apateon specimens shown in Figures 2-5 and comparison with literature.

claim: The presence of very few bony trabeculae with no preferential orientation in the metaphyseal region of Apateon's long bones strongly supports the idea that ossification did not occur within a zone of columnar hypertrophic cartilage.
source: However, the presence of very few bony trabeculae, with no preferential orientation in the metaphyseal region of Apateon's long bones (Figures 2–5) strongly support the idea that the ossification did not occur within a zone of columnar hypertrophic cartilage.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of Apateon specimens shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: Bone elongation in Apateon was probably followed by mineralisation through globuli ossei as previously observed in the temnospondyl dissorophoid Doleserpeton.
source: Bone elongation was probably followed by mineralisation through globuli ossei as previously observed in the temnospondyl dissorophoid Doleserpeton (De Ricqlès, 1963; Figure 11).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations and comparison with literature.

claim: The metaphyseal trabecular meshes in the limb bones of Metoposaurus, Seymouria and Discosauriscus all exhibit the same fan-like pattern of longitudinal trabeculae.
source: On the contrary, the metaphyseal trabecular meshes in the limb bones of Metoposaurus, Seymouria and Discosauriscus all exhibit the same fan-like pattern of longitudinal trabeculae.
evidence: This is based on observations of these specimens.

claim: The fan-like pattern of longitudinal trabeculae implies that the growth plate comprised longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cells where endochondral ossification occurred through columnar cartilage-to-bone substitution.
source: This implies that the growth plate comprised longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cells where endochondral ossification occurred through columnar cartilage-to-bone substitution (Francillon-Vieillot et al., 1990; Kronenberg, 2003) as seen in turtles and crocodiles (e.g. Haines, 1938; Haines, 1942), lepidosaurs (e.g. Haines, 1969), dinosaurs (De Ricqlès, 1968; Horner et al., 2000; Horner et al., 2001), birds (e.g. Horner et al., 2001) and mammals (e.g. Jacenko et al., 1993; Figure 11).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations and comparison with literature.

claim: The fan-like trabecular configuration can be greatly remodelled in extant amniotes.
source: Although this fan-like trabecular configuration can be greatly remodelled in extant amniotes, it is only slightly remodelled here in the adult Seymouria and subadult Discosauriscus (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is based on comparison between extant amniotes and fossil specimens.

claim: The fan-like trabecular configuration is only slightly remodelled in the adult Seymouria and subadult Discosauriscus.
source: Although this fan-like trabecular configuration can be greatly remodelled in extant amniotes, it is only slightly remodelled here in the adult Seymouria and subadult Discosauriscus (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is based on observations of specimens shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: The amniote-like long-bone elongation is more commonly distributed than previously thought.
source: Therefore, our study shows that the amniote-like long-bone elongation is more commonly distributed than previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Amniote-like long-bone elongation is not restrained to the appendicular skeleton of amniotes.
source: It is not restrained to the appendicular skeleton of amniotes – including Discosauriscus and Seymouria (as demonstrated here), Ophiacodon, Dicynodon and some kannemeyeriids (De Ricqlès, 1972; Haines, 1938), marine reptiles, Plesiosaurus and Nothosaurus (Haines, 1938) – neither to that of stem tetrapods (Kamska et al., 2018; Sanchez et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016; Figure 11).
evidence: This is supported by observations from this study and citations.

claim: This study demonstrates for the first time that certain temnospondyls like Metoposaurus elongated their appendicular skeleton like amniotes.
source: Indeed, our study demonstrates for the first time that certain temnospondyls like Metoposaurus also elongated their appendicular skeleton like amniotes (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: Endochondral ossification based on the mineralisation of longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cartilage is a primitive process for the elongation of the appendicular skeleton in tetrapods.
source: We can confidently conclude that (1) endochondral ossification based on the mineralisation of longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cartilage is a primitive process for the elongation of the appendicular skeleton in tetrapods and that (2) ossification through globuli ossei is restricted to a limited group of stem- and crown-batrachians (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Ossification through globuli ossei is restricted to a limited group of stem- and crown-batrachians.
source: We can confidently conclude that (1) endochondral ossification based on the mineralisation of longitudinal columns of hypertrophic cartilage is a primitive process for the elongation of the appendicular skeleton in tetrapods and that (2) ossification through globuli ossei is restricted to a limited group of stem- and crown-batrachians (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The mineralisation processes in extant amphibians and amniotes largely differ in their timing and microstructural relationships.
source: The mineralisation processes in extant amphibians and amniotes largely differ in many points: (1) their timing and microstructural relationships (i.e. ossification dependant on a calcified scaffold in amniotes, Amizuka, 2012, but not in amphibians, Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001), (2) their initiation (i.e. stacks of hypertrophic cells in amniotes, Lüllmann-Rauch, 2015, versus isolated hypertrophic cells in amphibians, De Ricqlès, 1965; Quilhac et al., 2014) and (3) their molecular mechanisms (i.e. collagen type X secreted in amniotes, Gudmann and Karsdal, 2016; versus fibrillar collagens in amphibians, Quilhac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

source: The most parsimonious evolutionary scenario therefore suggests that stem tetrapods were able to produce globular calcified cartilage although they were elongating their bone through a columnar configuration (Figure 11).

claim: Long-bone elongation exclusively based on the intensive production of globuli ossei would have been a derived feature emerging within temnospondyls and restricted to extant batrachians and their close dissorophoid temnospondyl relatives.
source: Long-bone elongation exclusively based on the intensive production of globuli ossei would have been a derived feature emerging within temnospondyls and restricted to extant batrachians and their close dissorophoid temnospondyl relatives (e.g. Apateon and Doleserpeton).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations.

claim: Within amniotes, the globular calcification of the cartilage would have drastically reduced to be fully abandoned to the benefit of an exclusive columnar elongation.
source: Within amniotes – including stem amniotes – the globular calcification of the cartilage would have drastically reduced to be fully abandoned to the benefit of an exclusive columnar elongation (Figure 11).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations.

claim: Large aquatic animals usually produce a large amount of globular calcified cartilage to balance their buoyancy or in extremely retarded developmental conditions, such as paedomorphosis.
source: Two exceptions persist in amniotes: (1) large aquatic animals usually produce a large amount of globular calcified cartilage to balance their buoyancy or in extremely retarded developmental conditions, such as paedomorphosis (e.g. pachy-osteosclerotic amniotes, De Buffrénil et al., 2008; De Ricqlès and De Buffrénil, 2001; crocodiles, Haines, 1938), (2) diseased amniotes can have osteosclerotic problems which result in the production and retention of globuli ossei (Gussen, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Diseased amniotes can have osteosclerotic problems which result in the production and retention of globuli ossei.
source: Two exceptions persist in amniotes: (1) large aquatic animals usually produce a large amount of globular calcified cartilage to balance their buoyancy or in extremely retarded developmental conditions, such as paedomorphosis (e.g. pachy-osteosclerotic amniotes, De Buffrénil et al., 2008; De Ricqlès and De Buffrénil, 2001; crocodiles, Haines, 1938), (2) diseased amniotes can have osteosclerotic problems which result in the production and retention of globuli ossei (Gussen, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In diseased amniotes, the production of globuli ossei is not solely located in the epiphysis and does not play any role in the elongation process of limb bones.
source: In such cases, the production of globuli ossei is not solely located in the epiphysis and does not play any role in the elongation process of limb bones.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about diseased conditions.

claim: Amniotes keep the ability to produce globuli ossei although they do not allocate them to the limb-bone elongation process.
source: Even though these cases reflect derived and/or rare conditions, they show that amniotes keep the ability to produce globuli ossei although they do not allocate them to the limb-bone elongation process.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of exceptional cases.

claim: It was hypothesised that a large number of globuli ossei would be associated with a slow limb-bone endochondral ossification and development.
source: It was hypothesised that a large number of globuli ossei would be associated with a slow limb-bone endochondral ossification and development (De Ricqlès, 1972; Haines, 1938).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The observations herein clearly show that long-bone developmental dynamics does not seem to be the leading or unique factor for performing one or the other of the elongation and calcification processes.
source: The observations contained herein clearly show that long-bone developmental dynamics does not seem to be the leading or unique factor for performing one or the other of the elongation and calcification processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's observations.

claim: The stem tetrapods Hyneria, Eusthenopteron and Acanthostega exhibit the characteristics of a slow appendicular development but only produce very few globuli ossei.
source: Indeed, the stem tetrapods Hyneria, Eusthenopteron and Acanthostega (with a humerus remaining cartilaginous for several years), all exhibit the characteristics of a slow appendicular development (and slow somatic development as a whole for Eusthenopteron and Acanthostega [Sanchez et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016]) but only produce very few globuli ossei (Kamska et al., 2018; Sanchez et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Hyneria, Eusthenopteron and Acanthostega all present an obvious longitudinal metaphyseal spongiosa strongly supporting the development of a hypertrophic columnar cartilaginous growth plate.

evidence: This is based on observations from the literature.

claim: Seymouria, Discosauriscus, and Metoposaurus exhibit the same trabecular pattern despite different somatic sizes and distinct ecologies.
source: Both seymouriamorphs, Seymouria and Discosauriscus, and the temnospondyl Metoposaurus exhibit the same trabecular pattern despite different somatic sizes (skull length of an adult Seymouria estimated to 9.5 cm, Berman et al., 2000; skull length of a possibly adult Discosauriscus estimated to 6.2 cm, Klembara, 1995; Klembara, 2009; skull length of an adult Metoposaurus estimated to 40–50 cm, Sulej, 2007) and distinct ecologies (Seymouria and Discosauriscus being (supposedly) terrestrial, Berman and Martens, 1993; Klembara, 2009; Klembara and Meszároš, 1992; and Metoposaurus being aquatic, Schoch and Milner, 2000).

claim: Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001 observed a late calcification and late ossification of the trabeculae in Rana catesbeiana which did not contribute to the bone elongation.
source: Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001 investigated the limb-bone ossification of the amphibian Rana. They observed a late calcification and late ossification of the trabeculae in Rana catesbeiana which did not contribute to the bone elongation (Felisbino and Carvalho, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The microanatomy of Metoposaurus, Seymouria, and Discosauriscus revealed tubular structures which can be confidently interpreted as marrow processes.
source: The microanatomy of the other taxa (Metoposaurus, Seymouria, Discosauriscus), however, could be investigated in 3D using PPC-SRµCT. It revealed tubular structures which can be confidently interpreted as marrow processes (on the basis of their shape, size and location in the bone), as seen in extant crocodiles (Haines, 1938).
evidence: This is based on observations and comparison with literature.

claim: The marrow processes in Metoposaurus, Seymouria, and Discosauriscus differ from the closed system observed in the stem tetrapod Eusthenopteron.

source: The tip of the marrow process forming a tube penetrating the hypertrophic cartilage of the growth plate in crocodiles is located at the level of the mineralisation front, and in mammals, that is at the base of the calcifying layer of hypertrophic cartilaginous cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and referenced to Figure 1A.

source: The tip of the marrow process plays a role in initiating endochondral ossification with marrow cells releasing lytic enzymes that degrade the calcified cartilaginous matrix (Suzuki et al., 1981).

claim: The centralisation of the vascular and marrow systems is crucial for haematopoiesis to occur in long bones.
source: The centralisation of the vascular and marrow systems is therefore crucial for haematopoiesis to occur in long bones (Tanaka, 1976).

claim: The full compartmentalisation of the marrow processes in Eusthenopteron would probably prevent the formation of a centralised vascular network.
